title: River flow or rainfall? Writing parametric flood triggers from global data, tested gauge by gauge in the Guadalquivir basin, Spain
description:
A parametric flood policy pays when an index crosses an agreed trigger. Where a river has no gauge, the index has to come from global data: a flood model's river flow, or rainfall. We test both against 14 river gauges in the Guadalquivir basin, Spain (583–16,166 km², water years 1985–2022, 286 gauge-years), in the region where a recent industry study compared four ways of setting rainfall triggers for drought cover. Flood-frequency curves were fitted by L-moments (GEV and log-Pearson III) to the annual maxima of the gauges, of the GloFAS reanalysis and of catchment rainfall from NASA POWER, and 1-in-T triggers were scored year by year against the floods the gauges measured. The model's 10-year flood is 0.22 of the gauged one at the median gauge, so a trigger written in m³/s from the model caught only 6 of 60 1-in-5 flood years (Peirce skill 0.06); written as the model's own 1-in-5 level it caught 30 (Peirce 0.38; McNemar p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁷). Set from each gauge's own record, as a quantile, a return period or a share of the mean annual maximum, triggers on the same index performed alike; one absolute level shared by all gauges paid in 0% to 78% of years from one gauge to the next and lost skill (Peirce 0.23). Storm rainfall (the wettest three days) was a weaker index than river flow (23 of 60, Peirce 0.26); the October–April rainfall total matched it (31 of 60, Peirce 0.39), and the two disagreed on few flood years (6 against 7). Requiring both to pass cut false payouts from 47% to 29% of payouts, at the cost of 6 flood years. Basis risk remained high in every design, and the rank correlation of the gauge's annual maxima with the index's predicted where it would be (Spearman ρ = 0.80 across gauges for river flow). Triggers from global data should be set from each site's own record, written in the index's own terms, screened with local evidence and calibrated before they enter a contract. Data, code and a notebook that reproduce every number are published with this paper.

The record holds the research paper, a companion technical report (KAI-Hydro KH-TR-2026-01) and the data package: derived annual maxima at 14 CEDEX gauges, at their GloFAS cells and of catchment rainfall from NASA POWER; the catchments behind the rainfall; the result files and figures; a notebook that reproduces the river-flow results; and the scripts that rebuild the derived data from the sources, compare the four ways of setting a trigger on river flow and rainfall, and build the documents. Interactive version with maps: https://kai-water.charkaks0.workers.dev/case-guadalquivir.
notes: Gauge data: Fuente: CEDEX, Anuario de Aforos 2021-2022 (MITECO); raw CEDEX files are not redistributed, only derived annual maxima. Global model: contains modified Copernicus Emergency Management Service information 2026 (GloFAS 4.0), via the Open-Meteo flood API (CC BY 4.0). Rainfall: data obtained from the NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project, funded through the NASA Earth Science/Applied Science Program. Catchments: HydroBASINS (Lehner and Grill, 2013). The four-way comparison follows Model Library (2026), Four ways to set a parametric trigger, tested on Andalucía rainfall and yields. Code: MIT. Text, figures and derived data: CC BY 4.0.
